Hi {{ firstname }},

Six weeks is the point where a system starts telling you how it's going to age. Two things worth checking this week.

The front perimeter. Hold it to the light and look along the very front edge. Fine splits there are normal wear, but they spread. Catching one now is a repair; catching it in a month is a replacement.

The knots at the crown. If hair is shedding faster than it was, that's usually cleaning technique rather than a fault — too much friction on the base.

Where you are in the cycle: most systems run three to six months. At six weeks you're roughly a third through, which means now is the time to be maintaining, not replacing.

Reply with a photo if anything looks off and I'll tell you what I'm seeing.

Vincent

[Hero - Text-led]
Your 30 / 60 / 90 day maintenance calendar.

[Text - Opening]
Hi {{ firstname }},

You've had your system about a week. This is the right moment for the maintenance schedule, because the habits you set now are the ones that stick.

[List - Questions: 30/60/90 checkpoints]
Every 7–14 days — full removal, clean the base, clean your scalp, reapply. Don't stretch this. Adhesive left too long is the single most common cause of base damage.

Every 30 days — deep clean. Solvent soak, gentle brush along the knots, air dry flat. Never wring it.

Every 60 days — inspect the perimeter. Lace goes at the front edge first. Catching a small tear here is a repair; missing it is a replacement.

Every 90 days — assess honestly. Most systems have a usable life of three to six months depending on wear and care. Knowing where you are in that cycle means you're never caught out.

Two things shorten a system's life more than anything else: heat styling directly on the base, and sleeping in it without a wrap. Neither is forbidden. Both cost you weeks.

Body:
[Hero - Text-led]
The four products that actually matter.

[Text - Opening]
Hi {{ firstname }},

Three weeks in, most people ask the same question: what do I actually need to buy, and what's marketing?

The honest short list:

A dedicated adhesive remover. Not acetone, not household solvent. This is the one product where the cheap option genuinely damages the base.

A sulphate-free shampoo. Sulphates strip the knots and loosen the ventilation over time.

A soft-bristle looped brush. Standard brushes catch the knots and pull hair through the base.

A scalp prep wipe. Cheap, and it roughly doubles how long a bond holds.

That's it. You do not need a leave-in, a serum, or a heat protectant unless you style with heat.

If you already have equivalents that work, keep using them. I'd rather you had a system that lasts than a bigger order.

Vincent

The question worth answering: same again, or change something?

[Text - Opening]
Hi {{ firstname }},

If you've been curious about hair systems but never quite understood them, here's the simple version — no jargon, no sales angle. There are only four parts that matter: the base, the hair, the attachment, and the routine. Everything else is detail.

[Photo - Founder note]
I explain this to someone new nearly every day. The base is the biggest decision — it determines how natural the system looks, how breathable it feels, and how long it lasts. Get that right and the rest follows. — Vincent

[Comparison]
Lace — most natural at the hairline, most breathable, shortest life.
Poly (skin) — most durable, easiest to clean and reattach, slightly less invisible up close.
Hybrid — lace front for the hairline, poly at the sides and back. Most people end up here.

[Timeline: how it works]
1. The hair — hand-tied into the base, matched to your colour, density and length. The goal is proportional and natural for your age, not "too perfect"
2. The attachment — tape or adhesive; properly done, it holds through workouts, swimming, wind and sleep
3. Daily — wash and style like natural hair (5 minutes)
4. Every 2–4 weeks — remove, clean scalp and base, reattach (30–45 minutes)
5. Every 3–6 months — replace the system

No surgery, no chemicals, no downtime.

[Text - Masthead]
Hair Solutions Co. — Education

[Text - Opening]
Hi {{ firstname }},

The most common question we get, by a wide margin: which base should I choose?

Most answers you'll find online are really product pitches. Here's the version that isn't.

There is no best base. There's only the trade-off, and it's the same one every time: the more realistic a base looks, the thinner and more fragile it is. Everything else — brand names, marketing terms, price tiers — sits downstream of that single trade-off.

So the useful question isn't "what's best?" It's "which do I care about more: the most natural possible hairline, or a system that survives my life?"

[Column - Image and text]
{{ image: close-up comparison of base constructions at the hairline }}
Left: Swiss lace at the hairline. Right: skin at the same angle. Both read as scalp from conversation distance — the difference is what each costs you in lifespan and routine.

[Comparison]
Lace (Swiss, French) — most natural hairline, breathable, scalp shows through the mesh. 3–6 months.
Skin (Nano 0.03mm → Dura 0.12mm) — clean shaved-scalp illusion, easiest to attach and remove. 1–8 months depending on thickness.
Mono (Mono Pro) — most durable, natural movement, comfortable for daily wear. 5–8 months.
Hybrid (Lace Edge, Mono Fusion LF, Thin Skin LF) — lace hairline with a PU perimeter for secure bonding. 3–6 months.

A rough rule that holds up: if you're new and nervous about detection, start lace at the front. If you're active, sweat a lot, or want the simplest routine, start skin or hybrid. If you want maximum life per unit, Mono Pro.

[FAQ]
Can I switch base types between orders? — Yes. Most customers adjust the spec on order two and lock it by order three.
Will people see the base? — Not at conversation distance, if the density is graded properly. The spec matters more than the base.
Do I need a consultation first? — No, but it removes the guesswork. It's free and there's no obligation.

[Text - Masthead]
Hair Solutions Co. — Education

[Text - Opening]
Hi {{ firstname }},

Here's the mistake almost everyone makes on their first order: they buy more hair than they ever had.

It's understandable. You've been missing hair for years — of course "full" sounds right. But a 40-year-old with the density of a 20-year-old doesn't read as lucky. It reads as wrong, even to people who can't say why. Density is the #1 reason systems get noticed — not the base, not the colour. The amount of hair.

[Column - Image and text]
{{ image: the same system at 90% vs 65% density, on the same head }}
Same base, same colour, same cut. The one on the right is 25 points lighter — and it's the one nobody looks twice at.

[Text - Base type guidance]
How to think about it:

- Match the hair you'd have if you'd never lost it — at your age, not at 20. That's the whole rule.
- Density is graded, not flat. A believable system runs lighter at the hairline and temples, fuller through the mid and crown. A flat, uniform density is what makes a front look like a wall.
- Rough ladder: 60–65% reads light and mature · 70–80% is the natural range for most men 30–50 · 90%+ only holds up on younger faces — and even then, graded.
- When in doubt, go one step lighter. You can add density on the next order; you can't subtract it from this one.

[FAQ]
Can density be adjusted after I order? — Not on the unit itself; a barber can thin it slightly, but it's better specced right. Most customers dial it in by order two.
What do most men actually order? — Medium (70–80%). It's our most reordered spec by a wide margin.
What about the hairline specifically? — Ask for a graded, slightly irregular front. It's on the spec sheet for a reason.

[Text - Opening]
Hi {{ firstname }},

Every so often someone asks why a system takes 3–4 weeks when a wig ships tomorrow. Fair question. This email is the answer — a walk through what actually happens between your spec sheet and your door.

[Text - Section: how a system gets made]
1. The spec sheet becomes a pattern. Your base type, size and hairline shape get cut before any hair is touched. If the consultation flagged an irregular hairline or temple recession, it's built in here — not styled in later.

2. Colour is matched against a physical ring, not a photo. Screens lie. Grey percentage is counted per zone, because real grey doesn't distribute evenly.

3. The hair goes in by hand — knot by knot. Ventilation is the slow part. Direction matters: crown hair grows differently to hairline hair, and a system knotted flat looks combed even when it isn't. The hairline gets the finest knots and the lightest grading, because it's the part everyone sees first.

4. It gets checked against the spec, not against "looks fine." Density per zone, colour under two light sources, hairline placement. If it misses, it doesn't ship.

That's the whole reason for the wait. Nothing on a shelf, nothing pre-made and relabelled. A system built to a spec takes the time the spec takes.

Vincent Laroche
Founder, Hair Solutions Co.

[Text - Masthead]
Hair Solutions Co. — Education

[Text - Opening]
Hi {{ firstname }},

When a system gets noticed, it's almost never the hair. It's the line the hair starts on.

Three giveaways, in order of how often we see them:

1. Too straight. Real hairlines are irregular. A ruler-clean front edge is the single fastest tell there is.
2. Too dense. The front of a real head of hair is its lightest zone — fine hairs first, fuller behind. A front that starts at full density starts like a wall.
3. Too low. Grown men don't have the hairline they had at 17. A low, closed hairline on a 45-year-old face doesn't read young — it reads wrong.

None of these are fixed by spending more. All of them are fixed on the spec sheet.

[Column - Image and text]
{{ image: two fronts side by side — straight/dense/low vs irregular/graded/age-appropriate }}
Same base material on both. The difference is entirely in how the front was specced.

[Text - Base type guidance]
What to actually ask for:

- A soft, irregular front — it's a standard spec-sheet option, not a custom favour.
- Graded density at the hairline — finest knots and lightest hair at the leading edge, stepping up behind.
- Age-appropriate placement — a rough rule: about four fingers above the brow ridge, with slight temple recession. If you have photos of yourself from before, send them with your consultation — they beat any formula.
- Lace at the front if detection is your top concern — it's what the mesh construction is for.

[FAQ]
Should the knots be bleached? — At the hairline, usually yes on darker hair — it removes the dot pattern at the roots. Elsewhere it trades durability for nothing you can see.
Can you copy my old hairline? — Yes. Photos from before are the best spec input we get.
What if my last system's front looked fake? — Almost always one of the three above. Reply with a photo and we'll tell you which.

[Text - Opening]
Hi {{ firstname }},

Most systems don't wear out. They get worn out — by advice that sounds sensible and isn't. Half the "tips" circulating in forums cost you months of lifespan.

Here are the ones we see doing the most damage, next to what actually happens.

[Column - Image and text]
{{ image: two systems after 4 months — one cared for correctly, one washed daily with the wrong products }}
Same system, same age. The difference is entirely routine.

[Comparison] — myth vs reality
"Wash it daily like real hair" — Daily washing strips the knots. 2–3 times a week with a sulfate-free wash is the honest ceiling.
"More adhesive = stronger hold" — More adhesive means more residue, harder removal, and a shorter base life. Thin, even coverage holds better.
"Any remover works" — Alcohol-heavy removers dry the base until it cracks. Use one matched to your adhesive.
"Brush it into place when wet" — Wet hair pulls at the knots hardest. Pat dry, then style.
"Sleep prep is optional" — Friction is the silent killer. A minute of prep (or a smoother pillowcase) buys real weeks.

None of this adds routine time. It just replaces the wrong five minutes with the right five.

[FAQ]
How often should I deep-clean the base? — Roughly monthly — residue build-up, not dirt, is what usually forces early retirement.
Can a barber help with upkeep? — Yes — more work with systems than you'd expect. Cutting it dry while worn is the norm.
What single change buys the most lifespan? — The remover. It's the cheapest fix on this list and the most commonly wrong.
